summary.value: This paper studies the probabilistic bisection algorithm (PBA) for noisy 1-D threshold/root finding and proves it achieves geometric convergence for a fixed (non-Bayesian) ground truth. The main result (Section 2.2, Theorem 1) shows E|θ̂n−θ*| ≤ 3e−Cn for a constant C depending only on the noise level p∈(0,1/2), matching the optimal noiseless binary search rate. The analysis hinges on new tools that directly characterize PBA’s query dynamics (Subsection 2.3): two propositions (Propositions 1–2) establish that a carefully chosen ratio of posterior masses Mn forms a supermartingale that decays exponentially while the queries oscillate across the truth with linearly many crossings in expectation. The proof technique departs from prior discretized/Bayesian analyses that rely on location-independent expected improvements (Eq. 3), and instead tracks location-dependent updates via posterior mass partitions and stopping-time arguments. The paper also treats more general noise models with error rate at most p (Appendix B). Beyond 1-D, it constructs a PBA-based estimator for Hölder-smooth decision boundaries with nearly minimax L1 rates (Appendix C, Theorem 2), and proves an exponential L1 rate for linear boundaries (Theorem 3). Simulations (Appendix D, Figure 1) illustrate the exponential error decay and the dependence of the constant on p.

strengths.value:
1. Resolves a concrete open question with a sharp result. Section 2.2 (Theorem 1) proves geometric convergence in the fixed-truth setting, E|θ̂n−θ*| ≤ 3e−Cn, with C depending only on p. The paper explicitly argues this rate matches noiseless binary search (lines 091–095), settling the question of whether PBA’s empirical efficiency persists under noise.

2. Novel, location-aware analysis of query dynamics. Subsection 2.3 introduces a fine-grained partition of the domain I1/I2/I3 and ties query locations to posterior mass via the median property Pn(Xn+1)=1/2 (Eq. 4). This departs from prior analyses that rely on location-independent drift (Eq. 3) and that “breaks down” for the original PBA (lines 210–215).

3. New supermartingale and stopping-time machinery tailored to PBA. The definition of Mn = a(3)n/a(2)n (Eq. 7) is carefully chosen to recover monotonicity in expectation (Remark 3). Proposition 1 shows exponential decay of Mn via log-supermartingale increments verified case-by-case (Case 2 and 3 in “Proof of Proposition 1”), and Azuma–Hoeffding is applied after lower-bounding the number of effective decrease steps.

4. Quantified oscillation around the truth with linear crossing rate. Proposition 2 proves E(T) ≥ ηn for the number of truth crossings (Eq. 5), giving a precise and interpretable dynamic: queries “oscillate across the truth” with shrinking amplitude (Implications). This insight is new and operationally useful for understanding adaptive posterior-updating algorithms.

5. Robustness beyond the symmetric noise model. Appendix B extends the result to general responses with P(Y≠hθ*(X)) ≤ p, noting that the key contraction of E(Mi/Mi−1) improves as the error probability drops and that T remains Θ(n). This broadens applicability without altering the core analysis.

6. Careful handling of boundary cases and tight tail control. The proof of Theorem 1 reduces to an upper-tail bound (Eq. 2) and uses a gridding-plus-Markov argument (Appendix A). Corner cases θ*∈{0,1} are treated separately via Lemma 2, showing P(a(3)n ≤ e−C1 n) with the same exponential decay flavor.

7. Meaningful high-dimensional extensions with near-minimax guarantees. Appendix C constructs a practical grid-lines-plus-1D-PBA estimator and proves E||ĝn−g*||1 ≤ O((log n/n)^{α/(d−1)}) (Theorem 2), explicitly leveraging Theorem 1 in the sample allocation (Eq. 10–15). It also proves an exponential L1 rate for linear boundaries (Theorem 3), close to best possible in this structured setting.

8. Clear exposition that aids verification and reuse. The paper includes targeted remarks (Remark 2 on the role of a(j)i, Remark 3 on the design of Mn), a succinct proof sketch (Implications and “Proof Sketch” under Subsection 2.3), and a structured, stepwise proof of Proposition 1 (Steps 1–3). The algebraic checks (e.g., monotonicity of h(x) and the bound −ln 2 + H(p) < 0 in Case 3; Eq. 6 drift bounds) are explicit and easy to follow.

9. Empirical illustrations are consistent and informative. Appendix D (Figure 1) shows linear decay in log-scale across p∈{0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4}, and documents numerical limitations at very small errors—consistent with the proven exponential rates and the p-dependence of constants.

10. Conceptual tools likely of independent interest. The posterior-mass ratio Mn, the crossing-time process {τi} (Eq. 5), and the demonstration that improvement depends on query location (contrasting Eq. 3) provide a reusable template for analyzing other adaptive query algorithms under noise.

weaknesses.value:
1. Dependence on known noise level p. The update rules in Section 2.1 (eqs. (1)–(2)) require p as an input. The theory and the experiments (Appendix D, Figure 1) assume p is known, but many applications do not. Actionable: analyze robustness to misspecified p, or design an adaptive scheme that estimates p online (e.g., via occasional repeated queries) and prove that Theorem 1 still holds up to a controlled degradation.

2. Unjustified IID/optional-stopping steps in the core arguments. In the Proof of Proposition 2 the inter-crossing times Zi are stated to be IID with EZk ≤ z, and in the Proof of Proposition 1, Step 2.3, the indicators Rk are treated as IID Bernoulli with P(Rk=1)≥p. These independence claims are not derived from the dynamics (query locations depend on the full history). Actionable: replace the IID assertions with conditional drift bounds (E[Δ | history]) and apply optional stopping/Azuma–Hoeffding under bounded increments; explicitly state the filtration and verify the conditions. Alternatively, prove mixing/renewal properties that justify IID or apply a renewal-reward bound without independence.

3. Non-explicit constants and rate degradation from gridding/Markov. Theorem 1 states E|θ̂n−θ*| ≤ 3e−Cn, but Appendix A concludes with ≤ 3e−Cn/4 after “Choosing K = eCn/4.” The proof also introduces C6 = min{(1−2p)2ε2, ln 2 − H(p)} in Proposition 1 without propagating it to an explicit C(p) in the final bound. Actionable: carry constants through to provide a concrete lower bound on C(p) (in terms of ln 2 − H(p) and (1−2p)2), and, if possible, avoid the 1/4 loss by tightening the gridding/Markov step with a direct tail bound on |θ̂n−θ*|.

4. Lack of high-probability/sample-complexity guarantees. The main guarantee is in expectation (Section 2.2, Theorem 1). While Eq. (2) and (9) provide ingredients, the paper does not state a clean PAC-style bound P(|θ̂n−θ*| > ε) ≤ δ or its sample complexity n = O(log(1/δ)+log(1/ε)). Actionable: translate the tail control on a(3)n into a bound on |θ̂n−θ*| via the grid construction to give an explicit (ε,δ)-guarantee, aligning with the “noisy binary search” comparisons discussed in the Introduction (lines 054–060).

5. Missing explicit bounded-increment constants needed for concentration. In Proposition 1, Step 3, it is asserted that ln(Mi/Mi−1) have uniform absolute and variance bounds B1,B2, but these are not derived. Actionable: include explicit bounds (as functions of p) from the case analyses (Case 2 and Case 3) to validate Azuma–Hoeffding and to make the dependence of the exponent on p transparent.

6. “Optimality” claim lacks a matching lower bound in the fixed-truth noisy setting. The Abstract and Section 2.2 (lines 091–095) claim optimality by matching noiseless binary search. This matches the rate class but not necessarily the best possible exponent under noise. Actionable: either add an information-theoretic lower bound for any algorithm under P(Y≠hθ*(X))≤p, or explicitly qualify “optimal” as “matching the noiseless exponential rate class.”

7. Limited empirical validation of the key dynamic claims. Appendix D, Figure 1 shows only 1-D absolute error decay for four p’s up to n=100. It does not probe (i) the oscillation/crossing behavior central to Proposition 2 (Eq. (5)), (ii) boundary cases θ*∈{0,1} (Lemma 2), or (iii) robustness to the general noise model of Appendix B. Actionable: add plots of the expected number of crossings T vs. n, histograms of inter-crossing times, experiments with θ* near 0 or 1, and trials with heterogeneous error probabilities bounded by p. A comparison to the discretized BZ scheme (lines 065–070) would contextualize constants.

8. Prior sensitivity. All results are proved for a uniform prior (Section 2.1, f0(x)=1), and M0 in Proposition 1’s conclusion depends on (δ−θ*) via M0=(1−δ)/(δ−θ*). Actionable: extend the analysis to priors with densities bounded above/below on [0,1], to show the rate is prior-robust up to a constant factor depending on the prior’s envelope.

9. High-dimensional extension is purely theoretical and non-adaptive. Appendix C gives rates (Theorems 2–3) but no experiments, no computational complexity discussion, and assumes knowledge of α to set M and of p to set N. Actionable: (i) report a 2D synthetic study validating the L1 rates, (ii) state the computational cost in n and d of the grid-lines-plus-interpolation scheme, and (iii) discuss/adapt to unknown α (e.g., via multi-resolution selection) and unknown p.

10. Conservativeness near the critical noise p→1/2. The proof reveals key constants like ln 2 − H(p) and (1−2p)2 (Proposition 1, Case 3 and the definition of C6), which vanish as p→1/2, but the final theorem does not quantify this degradation. Actionable: present explicit bounds that show how C(p) decays as p→1/2, and consider simple variance-reduction tactics (e.g., occasional repeated measurements) within PBA to improve constants at high noise, along with a theoretical guarantee.

questions.value:
1. Constants and exponent in Theorem 1. Section 2.2 states E|θ̂n−θ*| ≤ 3 e−Cn, but Appendix A concludes with ≤ 3 e−Cn/4 after “Choosing K = eCn/4.” Please reconcile these and carry explicit constants through the proof. In Proposition 1 you define C6 := min{(1−2p)2ε2, ln 2 − H(p)}; can you provide an explicit C(p) in Theorem 1 in terms of ln 2 − H(p) and (1−2p)2 and remove or tighten the 1/4 loss due to the gridding/Markov step?

2. Justification of IID/renewal claims. In Proof of Proposition 2 you write “Z_i := τ_i − τ_{i−1} are IID” and in Proposition 1 Step 2.3 the indicators R_k are “IID Bernoulli” with P(R_k=1) ≥ p. Since query locations depend on the full history, please either (a) prove these IID statements with a renewal argument, or (b) restate them as conditional drift bounds E[R_k | filtration] ≥ p and use optional stopping/Azuma with bounded increments. Explicitly define the filtration associated with (X_i, Y_i, P_i).

3. Bounded-increment constants for concentration. Proposition 1 Step 3 invokes uniform bounds B1, B2 on |ln(M_i/M_{i−1})| and its variance. Please derive these bounds from the three case analyses (Case 1–3) as explicit functions of p, so the applicability of Azuma–Hoeffding is immediately verifiable and the dependence of the exponent on p becomes transparent.

4. Monotonicity of h(x) in Case 3. In the “Proof of Proposition 1,” Case 3 defines h(x) and argues h′(x) > 0 because 1 > 4p(1−p). Could you provide a clean lemma stating h is increasing on x∈(0,1) for all p∈(0,1/2), including boundary behavior at x→0,1? A short proof or figure would clarify this technical step.

5. Role of the prior. Section 2.1 assumes a uniform prior f0(x)=1 and Proposition 1 ends with M0=(1−δ)/(δ−θ*). How sensitive are your guarantees to the prior? Can you extend Theorem 1 to priors whose densities are bounded above/below on [0,1], quantifying the constant blow-up via the prior envelope?

6. Unknown or misspecified p. The updates in Section 2.1 (eqs. (1)–(2)) require the noise level p. How robust is PBA’s geometric convergence if the algorithm uses p′ ≠ p? Can you provide a theorem showing exponential convergence with a degraded constant when |p′−p| ≤ Δ, or propose an online estimator of p (e.g., via occasional repeated queries) and prove that Theorem 1 still holds?

7. High-probability/PAC bounds. You establish tail control for a(3)_n (Eq. (2), (9)). Can you translate these into a clean PAC-style bound P(|θ̂_{n}−θ*| > ε) ≤ δ and a corresponding sample complexity n = O(log(1/ε)+log(1/δ)) with explicit p-dependence? This would directly connect to the “noisy binary search” comparison (Intro, lines 054–060).

8. Step 2.2 probabilities in Proposition 1. The multi-step case analysis (Step 2.2) concludes that “with probability at least p” a down-crossing yields membership in G′2 ∪ G3 before the next down-crossing, under ε constraints. Please make the ε choices explicit (they appear as functions of p) and provide a rigorous lower bound on this probability, with a clear argument that dependencies across steps do not invalidate it.

9. Quantitative link between Propositions 1 and 2. You deduce E(N′2+N3) ≥ η′ n (Step 2.3) and then apply Azuma. Could you add a high-probability version (e.g., via Freedman’s inequality) showing N′2+N3 concentrates around its mean, and then propagate it to an explicit high-probability exponential decay bound for M_n with constants depending only on p?

10. Direct tail bound without gridding. The Appendix A proof uses a K-grid and Markov’s inequality to move from P(a(3)_n ≥ ε) to |X_{n+1}−θ*|. Is there a way to leverage the median property P_n(X_{n+1})=1/2 (Eq. 4) to obtain P(|X_{n+1}−θ*| > ε) directly in terms of a(3)_n (or similar) and thereby avoid the union bound over K and the 1/4 exponent loss?

11. Boundary and near-boundary behavior. Lemma 2 covers θ* ∈ {0,1}. Can you characterize how constants behave as θ*→0+ or 1− (e.g., via M0 dependence in Proposition 1)? A short lemma showing continuity of constants near the boundary would close this gap.

12. Empirical validation of oscillation. Proposition 2 implies E(T) ≥ η n for crossings (Eq. 5). Could you add plots in Appendix D of the observed T versus n (and the distribution of inter-crossing times) to corroborate this key dynamic, alongside Figure 1’s error plots?

13. High-dimensional algorithm details. For Theorem 2 (Eq. 10), please provide pseudo-code for the “grid-lines-interpolate” estimator, its computational complexity in n and d, and guidance on choosing M,N when α is unknown. Is a multi-resolution/Lepski selection feasible here? A brief discussion would improve the practical value.

14. Linear-boundary case constants. In Theorem 3 you depend on σmin(Z) from the anchor design. For the concrete choice in the proof (canonical basis plus origin), can you provide an explicit lower bound on σmin(Z) as a function of d to make C1 and c completely explicit?

15. Clarifying the stopping-time claim (lines 487–491). You state that a(1)_t will cross 1/2 both up and down at least once within n/2 steps with probability ≥ 1−e^{−C4 n} by Hoeffding. Please formalize this as a lemma: specify the martingale/submartingale used, the bounded increments, and the dependence of C4 on p.

16. Robustness to heterogeneous noise (Appendix B). The text argues that when P(Y≠hθ*(X)) ≤ p, the contraction in E(M_i/M_{i−1}) improves. Could you state a formal corollary of Proposition 1/Theorem 1 under this general noise model, with an explicit constant C(p̄) driven by the worst-case error rate?

17. Stronger concentration inequalities. Since you mention variance bounds B2, would using Bernstein/Freedman (instead of Azuma) in Proposition 1 Step 3 yield sharper constants (e.g., remove the ε dependence in C6)? A remark or appendix note would help quantify possible gains.

18. Experimental quantification of exponents. In Figure 1, could you report estimated slopes (linear fits on the log-scale) with confidence intervals for each p, and, if possible, extend n beyond 100 using higher-precision arithmetic to avoid underflow? This would numerically validate the p-dependence of the exponent suggested by ln 2 − H(p) and (1−2p)2.

19. Comparison to BZ and Bayesian analyses. Since Section 2.2 argues Eq. (3) “breaks down” for the original PBA (lines 210–215), could you include a small synthetic example or plot where the expected drift is positive or zero at certain locations, thereby illustrating the limitation of location-independent analyses?

20. Notation and minor edits. Please fix “PBS updates”→“PBA updates” in Section 2.1, remove stray symbols like “̸” and duplicated blocks around lines 054–071, and harmonize notation for sign/indicator and indices (i vs. t) to ease verification of the proofs.
